title: PDF Editing Skills
description: Reshape PDFs on-device with pdf_edit instead of a web converter or an app's UI.
instructions:
Never send a PDF to a web converter and never automate a PDF app's UI to reorganise pages. pdf_edit does it locally: the file never leaves the device, and there is no watermark or page limit.

What it does, all page-level:
1. operation='info' — page count, file size, page dimensions. Call this FIRST whenever you need a page range and do not already know how long the document is. Never guess a page count from the file name or size.
2. 'merge' — joins the 'inputs' array into one PDF, in exactly the order given. Confirm the order with the user when it is not obvious; a merge in the wrong order looks like data loss to them.
3. 'split' — one file per page, written as <name>-p1.pdf, <name>-p2.pdf … into 'output' (a directory, defaulting to the input's folder). For anything longer than a few pages, ask whether they really want every page as a separate file — extract_pages is usually what they mean.
4. 'extract_pages' — copies the pages named in 'pages' into a new PDF. This is the tool for 'just send me the invoice page' or 'pull out chapter 2'.
5. 'delete_pages' — the inverse; drops the named pages.
6. 'rotate_pages' — adds 90, 180 or 270 degrees clockwise. Rotation ACCUMULATES on whatever the page already had, so rotating twice by 90 lands at 180. Sideways scans are the usual reason.

Page numbers are 1-based and take ranges: '3', '1-3,7', '9-' (nine to the end), or 'all'.

Output rules that matter. Every operation writes a NEW file and leaves the input untouched, so an existing output path fails unless you pass overwrite=true — do not reflexively retry with overwrite after that error, since the file in the way may be one the user still wants. Pick a clearly derived new name instead (statement-p2.pdf, report-merged.pdf) and say where you put it. Editing in place is legitimate when the user explicitly asks for it: pass the same path as input and output with overwrite=true.

Password-protected PDFs need 'password'. Ask the user for it — never guess, and never try a list of likely passwords. Editing one is gated on purpose: pdf_edit CANNOT carry the protection over to the copy it writes, so the first attempt is refused and you must warn the user before retrying. Say it plainly — 'the edited copy will not be password-protected, anyone who has the file will be able to open it' — ask with the 'question' tool, and only pass confirmed=true once they have actually agreed. Never set confirmed=true pre-emptively or to clear the error: the whole point is that the user, not you, decides to give up the protection. These are usually bank statements, payslips and medical letters, which is exactly why it is not your call. Reading is unaffected — operation='info' and read_file need only the password.

The hard limit: pdf_edit CANNOT change what is printed on a page — no editing text, fixing a typo, filling a form, redacting a name, or replacing an image. A PDF stores glyphs at fixed coordinates with no paragraphs to reflow, so this is a property of the format, not a missing feature. When asked, say that directly and offer what does work: read_file extracts the text of a PDF for you to quote or summarise, and the page operations above cover reorganising. Do not fake it by rebuilding the document from extracted text — the result loses all layout, images and signatures while looking plausible.

Finding the file: PDFs usually live in /sdcard/Download, /sdcard/Documents or a WhatsApp media folder. Use glob (e.g. '/sdcard/Download/*.pdf') rather than asking the user for a full path they will not know.
